newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: New Moldovan leader vows unity, better Moscow ties.
newsitem.headline: New Moldovan leader vows unity, better Moscow ties.

text.p: Petru Lucinschi, the challenger who won Moldova's presidential election, is a former Kremlin apparatchik who promises better ties with Moscow and a more cautious, socialist approach to western-style economic reforms.
Lucinschi, who has been chairman of the former Soviet republic's parliament for three years, vowed to be president of all Moldovans, irrespective of their political loyalties.

"I will not be the president who divides people into good and bad, into democrats and communists, patriots and non- patriots," the former secretary of the Soviet Communist party central committee told a news conference on Monday.
"Only political and social stability will allow us to speed up reforms...and raise living standards," he said. He formally takes over from defeated President Mircea Snegur on January 15.
He said he would form a cabinet of "national trust" that could include social democrats, liberals, communists and others.
Lucinschi, 56, wants to rein in "savage capitalism", which he blames for casting many of Moldova's 4.3 million people into some of the worst poverty in Europe.
The tall, bespectacled Lucinschi has been critical of Snegur's bid to turn his back on Moscow in favour of ties with Romania, whose language is spoken by two in three Moldovans.
"I will use my ties in Moscow for the good of the country. Believe me, this is a very big advantage," he said on Monday.

The president-elect said he would use these connections not just to allow energy-starved Moldova to survive the winter by buying yet more Russian fuel on credit, but also to resolve major political issues.

Fears of submersion in a greater Romania prompted the Russian-speaking Dnestr region to break away in 1990 and fight a war in 1992 that was ended by Russian troops. Lucinschi has vowed to finalise a Moscow-brokered peace deal with the region that should eventually lead to the Russian forces going home.
A historian by training, the new president also said he wanted to preserve good relations with Bucharest and western partners in general, including agencies like the World Bank.
"We will continue integration in Europe, but will also strengthen traditional ties with our good neighbours -- Ukraine and Russia," said Lucinschi.
He recently said of Romania: "We are brothers, but each of us should look after his own household."

Active from an early age in the communist youth movement, the Komsomol, Lucinschi led Moldova's local communists before going on to become a secretary of the central committee of the party in Moscow in the final days of the Soviet Union.
Staying on after the break-up of the communist superpower, he was Moldova's ambassador to Russia from 1992 to 1993 before returning to Chisinau to chair the parliament.
He ran for the presidency as an independent left-of-centre social democrat and came second to Snegur with 28 percent of the vote in the first round on November 17.

He then won the backing of defeated Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli and his powerful Agrarian Party, as well as the communists. He was also strongly backed by state television, much of the press and even the Orthodox Church.
Snegur, a less exalted communist than Lucinschi in Soviet times, accused his opponent of "neo-communism" and of failing to protect the independence won under Snegur's leadership in 1991.
Lucinschi, however, has never tried to disavow his communist career during the Soviet era.
"My past is well-known, and I don't try to erase it or reject old friends," he wrote, taking care to add: "I never sent people to Siberia or prisons."
